title: How ‘Boys Love’ Conquered Asia
author: R. Taggart Murphy
content:
![How ‘Boys Love’ Conquered
Asia](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-21-at-12.29.41
---PM.png)

In the last week of July, two incidents involving disruptive Chinese fans of a
genre of Asian media triggered something close to a crisis in international
relations. Security personnel had forcibly removed a Chinese woman from an
event in Bangkok. Patrons of this type of event, known as a "fan meet," pay
considerable sums to see their favorite entertainers in person, hear them
being interviewed, and watch them perform song-and-dance routines. Tens of
thousands of Chinese went online to accuse the Thais of mistreatment of and
discrimination against Chinese fans.

Four days later, a group of what appeared to be largely Chinese fans mobbed
two Chinese actors at Bangkok's Suvarnabhumi Airport. Thailand's foreign
minister was forced to step in, while embassies in both Bangkok and Beijing
attempted to calm outraged feelings. Although the controversy was extensively
covered by media in Thailand, China, Taiwan, and Hong Kong, nothing about
either incident appeared in mainstream Western outlets.

This lack of attention is especially noteworthy considering that one of the
viral media sensations of the past year in Western countries has been the
Canadian show _Heated Rivalry_ , a drama about gay hockey players. The show
attracted millions of viewers and the online equivalent of a spring snowmelt
of posts, reactions, and comments. But in Asia, filmed depictions of erotic
attraction and love between two males had in fact been drawing in tens of
millions of viewers and making lots of money since well before _Heated
Rivalry_ came along; it was shows in this genre that provoked the incidents in
Bangkok in July. But few in the Western critical establishment have paid
attention to this phenomenon.

The genre in question is known as "Boys Love" or "BL." It was invented in
Japan in the early 1970s by a group of women artists writing manga directed at
girls. These artists penned fantasies of impossibly beautiful boys with the
hots for each other, and in the process revolutionized _shojo manga_(comics
for girls). The new millennium saw the advent of filmed depictions of BL using
live actors. Largely set in offices rather than high schools, colleges, or
historical or mythical places, most of these shows starred established actors
(none of them openly gay), and did not feature boys even in minor roles.

So why are these shows called Boys Love dramas? Wouldn't they better be termed
"gay" or "LGBTQ" or "queer" programs? The answer lies with the creators and
the intended audience. Like the manga and anime in the tradition from which
they emerged, the majority of these dramas continued to be conceived by
(straight) women for women and girls.

In 2014, the first live BL drama appeared in Thailand. The show in question,
_Lovesick the Series_ , exploited the runaway popularity of Japanese BL manga
and anime among girls and young women and aimed, in the words of the scholar
Thomas Baudinette, to make "the Japanese BL elements legible to a Thai
consumer." Its creators followed the conventions of Thai media, including
background songs sung by the actors, extensive use of product placement in
lieu of disruptive commercials, and serialization. But for the first time ever
on Thai television, it featured a romantic relationship between two males as
the central plot pillar.

 _Lovesick_ 's success demonstrated to Thai media companies the potential
appeal and commercial possibilities of the genre, and over the next five
years, nearly a hundred BL dramas appeared on Thai television, a plurality of
them produced by GMMTV, a division of Thailand's largest media empire, with
many more financed by investors from China, where streaming of Thai BL dramas
became immensely popular.

> "GMMTV and its competitors constructed a new business model."

GMMTV and its competitors constructed a new business model. Live-action
Japanese BL dramas had been typically filmed on very tight budgets as a means
to boost the sales of the manga on which most of them were based. The shows
tended to air on late night television; if the producers and distributors even
bothered with overseas audiences, the shows were licensed to streaming
platforms such as GagaOOLa or Viki that in turn required viewers to pay for
subscriptions.

The Thais, instead, monetized the actors themselves, a practice they adapted
from South Korea. Building on the country's prior success in exporting
manufactured goods from automobiles to consumer electronics, Korean
entrepreneurs in the 1990s turned their attention to popular culture--in
particular, a form in which the Japanese had conspicuously failed to penetrate
Western markets: singing and dancing boy bands. They honed in on the talent
agency that had dominated Japanese pop music for two generations: Johnny and
Associates, whose founder "Johnny" Kitagawa had built an industrial machine
for the spotting of attractive boys and their fashioning into "idols" who
could and would electrify millions of besotted pubescent girls. Of course this
was not the first time in history that handsome young male musicians had
filled concert halls, theaters, and stadiums with screaming females, but no
one had ever done it on Kitagawa's scale. Through open auditions and informal
scouting, he recruited thousands of pre-teen and teenaged boys into his
workshop where they were drilled in singing, dancing, and stagecraft. Those
whom Kitagawa deemed most likely to succeed would debut in splashy events
backed by the full weight of his publicity machine which already, by the
1970s, was far and above the most formidable in Japan.

Kitagawa was dogged by allegations that he had sexually abused boys under his
management. A documentary released after his death brought these claims before
a wider audience, raising the uncomfortable possibility that Kitagawa's nose
for star potential was totally wrapped up in his sexuality.

Johnny's stars never found a fan base in the United States and Europe, despite
periodic attempts, but beginning in the 1990s, their Korean counterparts
managed to do so. The greater attention to the spit and polish of what was on
offer was one reason for the Koreans' success. But the deliberate and
systematic cultivation of global audiences was at least as important. The
Japanese had treated the outside world as an afterthought when it came to
cultural (as opposed to manufactured) products. Not so the Koreans. One key
factor lay in their early grasp of the internet's potential, something
Kitagawa had completely missed. With a mindset locked into the age of
television and print media and obsessed with maintaining control of his stars,
Kitagawa had deliberately suppressed online distribution of their songs and
performances. But in 2007, the Korean boyband Big Bang embraced Youtube; the
even more famous BTS would go on to use free online content as a means to
build a global fan base.

Perhaps the most fruitful--and certainly the most profitable--result of
Thailand's infatuation with both Japanese and Korean influences lay in the
adoption of methods the Koreans had used to globalize K-pop, but applying
those methods to actors in BL dramas rather than members of boybands. Between
2015 and 2020, GMMTV perfected the formula for a hit show: two handsome leads
falling in love with each other, an open declaration of love by one or both at
some point later in the series, a breakup near the end triggered either by
external events or internalized self-doubts, followed by a reconciliation and
a happy ending. While many of these recurring plot elements had their origins
in the Japanese genre, GMMTV modified things in a number of significant ways.
The more aggressive macho "top" (_seme_ in Japanese) vs. the more submissive,
boyish "bottom" (_uke_) tended to dissolve into a more egalitarian
relationship (egalitarian at least in an erotic sense; class tensions did
surface in many shows). Attraction was a matter of romance rather than overt
lust. Perhaps most importantly, external homophobia was no longer an issue.
Parents, friends, and colleagues were increasingly shown to be supportive and
if any stigma was felt, it was an internal feeling that had to be overcome.

In 2020, helped by the arrival of the pandemic that forced people indoors, the
Thai Boys Love model reached full fruition with the runaway hit _2gether: The
Series_. The plot borders on the preposterous, but the show was a massive
success thanks largely to the looks and charisma of the two leads. Its reach
extended far beyond Thailand: At one point, it generated more posts on Twitter
than any other television show anywhere and racked up total viewership in the
range of one billion (that's not a typo).

In the process, GMMTV had hit upon a formula for monetizing the success of
these shows: distributing BL dramas on easy-to-access free platforms such as
Line TV and YouTube while relying on product placement, celebrity
endorsements, and fan meets to generate revenue. That was the Korean boy band
model, but with a twist. GMMTV sought to monetize not simply the charisma of
the actors, but the idea of what Baudinette calls "homoerotic imagined
couples" who, following a successful debut, go on to appear together in live
concerts and "fan meets" while continuing to be cast as lovers in new shows
with no plot connection to the original drama.

After the success of _2gether: The Series_ , Thai studios issued dozens of BL
shows every year. No matter the theme or plot conceit--or how well or badly
made or how much or how little was spent on production--the love interest in
every one of these dramas centered on the relationship between two young
males. Programs such as _Bad Buddy_ , _Gelboys_ , and _ThamePo_ garnered tens
of millions of viewers, with a fan base extending far beyond Thailand's
borders to the whole of southeast Asia, China, and the subcontinent. Most
recently, Thai BL dramas have begun to reach Latin America, particularly
Brazil and Bolivia where, if GMMTV is to be believed, some of its programs
have claimed the number one spot on streaming sites.

Even Japan succumbed. Fans coined the term _tai-numa_ (literally, "Thai
swamp") referring to addictive infatuation with Thai BL dramas and their
stars. Annual visits by leading Thai BL stars pack concert halls and stadiums
while enterprising travel agencies organize tours by Japanese visitors to
sites in Thailand where some of the more popular dramas were filmed. Thailand
has thus joined Japan and South Korea in staking out a major claim on the
landscape of global popular culture. Hollywood doesn't yet realize it, or want
to realize it, but in the process cultural hegemony continues to leak from Los
Angeles and New York to Tokyo, Osaka, Seoul, and now Bangkok.

* * *

Why does the largely female fan base of Boys Love want to read about or watch
boys and young men (or even older men) in lust or in love with each other?
That many women enjoy gazing at attractive males is not news. Nor is it a
surprise that many women are aroused by depictions of handsome virile males in
the grip of uncontrollable passions awakening feelings of love and lust in the
object of said passions.

But why in East and Southeast Asia, and now South Asia and Latin America, did
male-on-male tales displace stories of male-on-female romance--or if not
displace them, come to compete with them on practically equal terms? One
common notion among observers attempting to explain the enormous popularity of
Asian BL among Asian women is that tales of male-on-male romance and lust feel
less threatening. As this account has it, patriarchal culture tells Asian
women they aren't supposed to have strong sexual feelings, but they do anyway;
watching an older and a younger guy go at it allows them to explore otherwise
taboo thoughts.

But there may be something more subtle at work that helps in understanding the
recent global reach of these dramas. Even a well-acted, well-written depiction
of heterosexual romance carries implicit expectations of who leads, who
yields, how desire is expressed. By contrast, many BLs allow viewers to
witness intimacy and vulnerability stripped of expectations of how people are
"supposed" to behave.

The open, unembarrassed, sentimentality of Thai BL is another key factor. At
the dramatic peaks of many shows, the action ceases while the soundtrack
features the lead actor singing of the emotions he is experiencing, often
accompanied on screen by a series of flashbacks. (An accomplished singing
voice forms a great boon to aspiring BL actors.) Thai BL inherited this
dramatic convention from _lakhorn_ (the traditional melodramatic soap operas)
but it is hardly unique to Thailand. Opera during the Baroque period
functioned in much the same way - action stopped while singers gave voice to
their emotions. Kabuki employs something similar--at peak dramatic moments,
the stage freezes, the actors strike extravagant poses, and off-stage
musicians articulate the emotions being felt.

> "This sort of thing also used to happen in Western popular culture."

This sort of thing also used to happen in Western popular culture. Hollywood
musicals once showed actors stopping to sing about what they were feeling. We
don't see that any more but it isn't because films such as the 1961 _West Side
Story_ or the 1965 _Sound of Music_ were box office bombs. Rather, the
Anglophone arts establishment seems to have been overtaken by a paralyzing
fear of sentiment without a protective wrapping of snark. Well, if Hollywood
can't figure out a way to allow viewers to revel in unabashed displays of
sentimentality, Bangkok will step in. Perhaps the pure sweetness goes down
more easily because it is being administered by two young men in love with
each other; one can watch, cry, thrill, and shake with ecstasy all the while
retaining hip "progressive" credentials.

That brings us to the most important matter that the global success of Thai BL
raises--and perhaps helps us grasp why the Western critical establishment
shies away from confronting what has been happening. The young male Thai stars
who pack stadiums from Mexico City to Yokohama to Manila, whose faces seem
plastered over all the Skytrain and subway cars in Bangkok and to pop up in
every second TV commercial on Thai television, got to where they are not
simply because of their looks and their talent, but because they made their
reputations on the pretense that they had been romantically and sexually
involved with other men and boys. One would have to reach back to Renaissance
Florence or Edo-period Japan and the cultural supremacy of the _wakashu_
(alluring youth) or, even farther, to ancient Athens and the worship of the
beautiful boy to find something comparable.

A number of scholars have begun to ponder the meaning and significance of
seemingly "queer" media attracting large audiences across national and
cultural borders, not to mention those of gender and sexual orientation. These
scholars argue that Thai BL represents an important new means of "queering"
heretofore heteronormative societies.

These theorists can certainly marshal plenty of evidence to support their
views, beginning with Thailand's approval of same-sex marriage in 2025, in
which the enormous popularity of BL almost surely played a role. Beyond
Thailand, any perusal of social media is enough to demonstrate that legions of
"queer" youngsters throughout Southeast Asia to Brazil and India find in these
shows affirmation for their feelings.

Yet the majority of BL fans still appear to be straight women and girls. While
the genre has moved beyond its women-writing-for-women roots and large numbers
of men (many of them openly gay) are involved in the production of the shows
in Thailand and elsewhere, there remains a strong female presence among the
writers and directors.

* * *

Are BL dramas "queer"? Thomas Baudinette explains that he is "inspired by the
seminal definition of queer from theorist David Halperin as 'whatever is at
odds with the normal, the legitimate, the dominant.'" Does BL constitute a
threat to the "hierarchical" and the "normative"? In China, the authorities
certainly think so: They have censored BL shows and blackballed the actors
while fining and imprisoning writers. What seems to bother a Chinese regime
reflexively suspicious of any mass movement that it does not control is not so
much the content of BL but the way the genre came out of nowhere and proceeded
to spawn millions of fans while no one in authority was paying attention.

> "Are BL dramas 'queer'?"

Another factor may be the CCP's worries about the plummeting Chinese birth
rate. A study of Chinese fans of Thai BL by a Taiwanese academic notes that
many report that their parasocial relationships with Thai BL actors provide
them with whatever intimacy they feel they need, and quotes a Chinese woman
saying "I have three husbands and two boyfriends--all in Thailand--I wish I
could tell my parents don't ﬁx me up with anyone." Meanwhile, a group of
conservative men in South Korea have called for the banning of BL because it
promotes unrealistic standards among Korean women for male beauty. Yet
birthrates had begun to fall in both South Korea and China well before the
surging popularity of BL in those two countries, and they have also fallen to
comparably low levels in countries such as Italy which have yet to join the
global BL boom. As for the idea that growing numbers of gay male fans of these
dramas will rush out, marry women, and father children if they are suddenly
deprived of the opportunity to watch ripped hunks and fetching youths
professing love for each other--well, it is palpably absurd.

More widely, any notion that declining birthrates can be blamed on these
dramas runs into the unavoidable reality that a large majority of at least the
live-action BL dramas depict loving romance in which genuine affection and
concern for the other trumps lust. Long-term commitment is seen as the goal,
not short-term sexual release. Cheating and dishonesty are the great no-nos,
and family and friends are usually depicted as loving and supportive. Indeed,
if it weren't for the sex of the principals, most live-action Asian BL dramas
would seem to champion precisely those values needed to reverse the decline in
birth rates. The values in question even include the promotion of family
formation with the curtain falling on pairs of lovers whose first act as they
build lives together is to adopt children.

That points to the discomfort many progressives feel over the genre: that it
caters to "regressive" female hunger for domesticity. Meanwhile, many gay male
activists contend that BL is little more than female wish fulfillment. In the
typical BL show, a teenaged boy or young man is awakened not to his sexuality
but to his love for another young male with whom, after the overcoming of
obstacles that make for necessary dramatic tension, he settles down for a life
of marital bliss. The notion that this fantasy has anything to do with the
actual lives of gay males is clearly a stretch.

But the core of progressive discomfort with the BL genre may lie less with the
fantasies on display than the challenge it poses to the notion of immutable
sexual identity or orientation. The idea that one is born "straight" or "gay"
did not exist in East and Southeast Asia until introduced by Westerners in the
nineteenth century. Gregory Pflugfelder began his magisterial book,
_Cartographies of Desire: Male-Male Sexuality in Japanese Discourse,
1600-1950_ , by noting that there was no single word for "homosexuality" in
the Japanese language during the era of the Tokugawa shoguns. The general
assumption was a kind of universal bisexuality, to use a term that likewise
would not have been easily understood. Men who did not like women or did not
like boys were considered somewhat odd.

So the women who invented BL as a genre in the pages of manga for girls in the
early 1970s were harking back to an understanding of sexuality that had only
recently been superseded by the introduction into Japan of Western notions of
homosexuality as a species of either sin or deviance, and the "homosexual" as
somehow standing apart from the rest of humanity. The underlying conceit of
most Thai, Chinese, and Japanese BL dramas is that lovers do not exist in a
separate category of human being. The Asian BL presentation of human sexuality
therefore complicates identity-based conceptual frameworks.

What messages does the BL genre tell its audiences that resonate so deeply?
Among them is that "affection between men is normal" to quote one of the more
perceptive commentaries. Another: people need close friends. Many Thai BLs
elevate the friend group to a status equivalent to family, and the working out
of the dynamics of the friend group, as opposed to those of the erotic
partnership, are at the core of many BL dramas. A third: the essential role of
male bonding in a healthy society. That Thai BL openly acknowledges and
celebrates the power of male bonding surely accounts for some of its global
reach.

Where the power and allure of BL can be seen most clearly lies in the way in
which BL places the forging of relationships firmly at the center of its
stories. Everything else--especially notions of identity and categorization
that have so obsessed the West in recent centuries--is relegated to side
issues, given a role to play only when they strengthen (or threaten) love,
friendship, and affection between human beings. People are not labels; over
and over again, in both subtle and blatant ways, BL dramas preach this
message.

The recent series _Ticket to Heaven_ uses the prism of the formative
institution of Western civilization, the Catholic Church, to underscore the
primacy of relationship formation--that without love, all else is "nothing" to
quote Paul's first letter to the Corinthians, referred to several times in the
drama. Set in a strict Catholic boys school, the story is predictable enough:
a straight laced, faithful honor student being groomed for.the priesthood has
his whole persona shaken by the arrival of a defiant "bad boy" transfer
student who intuits the "good boy's" repressed feelings and sets out to tear
down his walls. A crisis of faith ensues. The show does not shy away from
noting Catholic condemnations of lust, and of homosexual lust in particular.
But it juxtaposes these with what is palpably love--devotion to the other, and
the drama revolves around the clash between these two seemingly irreconcilable
commandments: to eschew all forms of overt homosexual eros and to place love
above all else.

To be sure, much of the drama could be construed as LGBT propaganda--among
other things, a hateful, homophobic religious fanatic of a father is
juxtaposed with an older saintly trans woman--and, in an unusual departure
from typical Thai BLs, one of the principals declares his orientation. But the
series avoids condemning the Church--just the reverse, in fact. The final
scene brings together most of the key characters at an ordination celebrated
in an atmosphere of faith, hope, and love, to choose words deliberately. The
director, colloquially known as Aof, is by his own account, a practicing
Catholic, albeit also married under Thai law to another man.

* * *

Perhaps the greatest significance of BL, particularly its Thai variant, lies
in its potential to undermine the categorization of human beings by erotic
urges. This category-undermining is clearly visible in the recent Thai show
_Class Crush Crisis_ (available on Netflix); indeed, it forms its underlying
theme. A mother distressed at her son's lack of devotion to his studies forces
him to transfer to an elite girls school that for the first time is accepting
a group of boys. Excitement runs high: the girls finally have cute boys right
at their proverbial fingertips; the boys, for their part, rejoice that landing
a girlfriend will just be a matter of identifying a girl who fits one's "type"
and then going after her. The school is a gossipy place with everyone glued to
their screens; rumors fly over who is with whom.

But all the rumors turn out to be false, and in the process, people are hurt.
Two of the girls are already in a relationship with each other. Other girls,
"educated" by a decade of BLs, start "shipping" two of the boys; while they
are right that homoerotic feelings exist among some of the boys, they get the
"ships" wrong. The central character, who starts a club for the boys both as a
form of self-protection and as a means for the boys to help each other find
girlfriends, is blinded by categories and rules--who is whose "type," people
shouldn't date those close to them--only to find it all blown up by his own
feelings and those of his friends not to mention the boy he finally has to
admit to himself he loves. He comes to understand that erotic feeling and
attraction to another is ultimately a mystery and that efforts to pin it down
with labels and categories risk turning people into things to be classified
rather than their own human selves.

_Class Crush Crisis_ is a feel-good romance featuring a gaggle of cute teens
(the actors are actually teenagers, not people in their twenties pretending to
be adolescents.) But the underlying message encapsulates the central values of
the BL genre--that people are not labels--and demonstrates its potential as an
art form that lies between the "queer" and the heteronormative.
